text: Most quantum tutorials live in a single flat script. A real quantum package needs the same kind of structure as any Python library, plus a few quantum-specific additions — like a place to keep noise models and backend configs separate from circuit logic.

In this lesson: a standard src-layout package structure adapted for quantum code, why circuit construction, execution, and analysis belong in separate modules, how to keep configuration like noise models and shot counts out of your code, and how pyproject.toml replaces the old setup.py for a modern installable package.

Here's a baseline layout for a small Grover's-search package called grover-toolkit. Under src, a circuits folder holds pure circuit-construction logic like the oracle and diffuser. A backends folder holds the abstract interface plus concrete simulator and hardware implementations, which Chapter 3 builds out fully. An analysis folder holds the statistics code that turns counts into a verdict. And a config folder holds default shot counts and noise models as data. The names matter less than the separation of concerns itself.

In a typical tutorial script, circuit-building, running, and printing counts all happen in the same ten lines. That causes three concrete problems in a real package. You can't unit-test circuit logic without executing a circuit, because construction and execution are the same function — every unit test secretly becomes an integration test. You can't swap backends without touching algorithm code, if the oracle file calls a specific provider directly. And you can't reuse analysis logic across algorithms if the same statistical check gets copy-pasted into every new script instead of living in its own module.

Modern Python packaging, and every current quantum SDK's own tooling, expects a pyproject.toml rather than the old setup.py. Here, dependencies get pinned exactly — qiskit at one-point-two-point-four, qiskit-aer at zero-point-fifteen-point-one — while a more ordinary library like numpy can stay on a looser range. That exact-pinning choice for the quantum SDKs specifically is deliberate, and lesson three explains why it matters more here than in most classical projects.
Next lesson goes deep on dependency management for quantum SDKs — why they churn faster than typical classical libraries, and how exact pins and committed lockfiles protect you from silent breaks.
